task
Developers can do the same thing on a site they're building. Start with what a visitor came to do.
Here, someone wants to find a pair of headphones and add them to their cart using a keyboard.
before
Give that task and the address to curbcut check. Kane opens the shop and tries it.
Watch the Add button. The keyboard skips right past it. The headphones stay on the shelf.
patch
Curb Cut proposes a small change. Let the button take focus, and let Enter activate it.
Kane tries again. Same shop, same headphones, same keyboard. This time there's an item in the cart.
gateFail
A developer can put that check into Claude Code, too. Here it runs when Claude tries to finish.
The first time, the button still skips the keyboard. The check fails and the Stop hook sends the work back.
gatePass
The developer fixes the button in the site itself. Claude reaches the end again.
This time Kane can add the headphones. The check passes and Claude can finish.
trust
A person using the extension can look at the evidence, too. Open Curb Cut on the page and choose the recording.
It shows what happened in the browser. You can see for yourself whether the menu opened.
names
On a new page, Jev looks at what each button does. Here on Meridiano, one opens the menu. Another opens search.
People checked the suggestions. Jev got 13 right out of 15. When it's unsure, it leaves the button alone.
report
If something else gets in the way, open Report a barrier. Describe what you were trying to do and where you got stuck.
The extension keeps a draft so you can review it.
retire
And when a site owner makes a repair, the browser should get out of the way. Kane tries the task with the extension's fix switched off.
The button works on its own. Curb Cut retires the fix.
end
The next person who comes to buy those headphones can use the keyboard from the start.
